rationale: Detecting and throttling automated abuse traffic while keeping service for normal users is resistance to attack.
Fingerprint enrolment and matching scan per session authenticate the researcher.
A signature makes later changes to the reservation detectable, which is integrity; the text does not state origin verification or non-repudiation.
Validating a device's signed certificate against a trusted issuer authenticates the device.
Ending the session and revoking the token limits misuse of a lost phone by a malicious party, per the session-termination rule.
Verifying the identity of every person and app before accepting commands is authentication.
Requires identity verification through valid credentials before commands are accepted.
Suspending a compromised session and refusing its commands contains an attack.
Re-confirming the clinician's identity with challenge questions is additional authentication.
Restricts modification to the owner (integrity) after successful identity verification (authenticity).
Storing a digest and flagging corruption on mismatch detects alteration of the record.
Protecting the encryption keys of patient files in a hardware vault safeguards confidentiality of the data.
Detecting and refusing a resubmitted transaction is replay protection.
Comparing the download with a published digest detects corruption or alteration of the file.
Regenerating the authentication code over the debit total keeps the record consistent and tamper-detectable.
Certificate verification authenticates nodes, and isolating nodes on repeated forged identities is a response to attack.
Encrypting stored statements so they cannot be read protects confidentiality.
A hash over each record lets the terminal detect tampering, which is integrity.
Requires verifying the profile owner (authenticity) before edits to stored data are allowed (integrity).
Granting a session only when credentials match a registered account is authentication.
Role-based view and edit capabilities restrict both reading and modification.
Restricting creation, editing and deletion of reference scenarios to one role limits who may modify data.
Verifying the service's certificate against its claimed domain authenticates the remote service.
Scanning plug-ins for malicious code and refusing infected ones resists malware.
Requires loaded values to match the source exactly and flags checksum differences, which is data integrity.
Terminating and invalidating the session on close limits exposure to session abuse, though no attacker is mentioned explicitly.
Encrypting client connections so traffic cannot be read in transit protects confidentiality.
Validating an account name and secret to identify each connection is authentication.
Only administrators may change the limit (integrity) and all others are denied viewing it (confidentiality).
Restricts who may change modification rights and stores a hash so alterations are detectable.
Computing and storing an integrity code over totals enables detection of alteration.
Locking the account after repeated failed sign-ins contains brute-force attempts (rule 1).
Rejecting inserts, updates and deletes by unprivileged accounts prevents unauthorised modification of data.
Only the owner may open (read) and trim or overwrite (modify) the capture, covering both reading and modification.
Allowing rule or firmware changes only with owner approval prevents unauthorised modification of programs and configuration.
A server-issued expiring one-time code required for login is an authentication factor.
Halting the payment and ending the session on a detected replay is a response to an attack.
Only the build manager may change shared project settings, restricting who can modify them.
Detecting and refusing alteration of the balance outside validated operations protects data integrity.
